text:
B: Hello, good evening. Can you hear me?
A: Yes, hello. I'm Tereza.
B: Tomasz. Nice to meet you.
A: Nice to meet you. Erm, Tomasz, is that Polish?
B: Yes, Polish, from Rzeszów. And you? I can hear a little accent also.
A: Czech, from Brno. So we are almost neighbours. [laughs]
B: Ah, very good. Neighbours in London as well, maybe. Where are you?
A: Leyton, East London. And you?
B: Hanwell, West. Other end of Central line.
A: Oh, the Central line. In summer it's like a sauna, I come to work completely melted.
B: Yes! This morning it was rammed, I was standing with somebody's elbow in my face. Usually I drive, I have company car, but today it was in for valeting.
A: Okay. What is your job, sorry?
B: Operations manager, facilities management. Office buildings, cleaning, security, maintenance. I have six supervisors. And you?
A: I'm clinical trials coordinator at a hospital. Paperwork, patient visits, samples. Very organised, very boring for other people. I just told the last person, he did film, and he has no release forms. [laughs]
B: [laughs] Ah, the young guy with the surfboard?
A: Yes. He's very nice, but I think he needs a spreadsheet.
B: For me, spreadsheets are life, to be honest. Budgets, contracts, everything. When contract renewal is coming, I'm checking my phone at midnight. My wife is angry with me.
A: Me too, before audits I can't sleep. I make a checklist, and then a checklist for the checklist. How long are you in London?
B: Eighteen years. I came at nineteen. First job, I was cleaning offices at night. Then porter, then supervisor, and now, you know, manager. Step by step.
A: Wow. That's a really big journey. I came eight years ago, just for one year. And now I am married to an Englishman, so... [laughs]
B: Ah, so you stay. My wife is Polish, we speak Polish at home, but our daughter, she's five, she answers me in English now. Every time. It's strange feeling, you know?
A: I can imagine. We don't have children yet, but I think about this, which language, where to live, near my mum or here. Sorry, that's a lot.
B: No, no, it's normal. I think about this also. Sometimes I feel not properly Polish, not properly British. Somewhere in the middle.
A: Yes, exactly that. When I go home, my brother says I talk like a tourist.
B: [laughs] My sister says the same. Do you go back for Christmas?
A: Yes, every year. Carp, potato salad, cookies. My mum starts baking in November.
B: Same, but with us it's the twelve dishes, and barszcz with uszka. And Midnight Mass, my mum makes us go. Is that okay, what I said? You are religious, maybe not?
A: Not really, no, but I like the traditions, the food especially. I saw your—
